name: Empress Lü
wd_description: Empress Regent of the Han dynasty (241–180 BC)
extract:
Lü Zhi (241 BC – 18 August 180 BC), courtesy name Exu (娥姁) and commonly known as Empress Lü (traditional Chinese: 呂后; simplified Chinese: 吕后; pinyin: Lǚ Hòu) and formally Empress Gao of Han (漢高后; 汉高后; Hàn Gāo Hòu), was the empress consort of Gaozu, the founding emperor of the Han dynasty. They had two known children, Liu Ying (later Emperor Hui of Han) and Princess Yuan of Lu. Lü was the first woman to assume the title Empress of China. After Gaozu's death, she was honoured as empress dowager and regent during the short reigns of Emperor Hui and his successors Emperor Qianshao of Han and Liu Hong (Emperor Houshao).
When Liu Bang was still humble, Lü Zhi became his consort. Lü Zhi was married to Liu Bang by her father in her early years and gave birth to a son and a daughter (Emperor Hui of Han, Liu Ying, and Princess Luyuan). Shortly after the Chu–Han Contention began, Lü Zhi and Liu Bang’s parents were captured by Xiang Yu. In the fourth year of the Han dynasty (203 BCE), due to unfavorable circumstances, Xiang Yu was forced to make peace with Liu Bang, and Lü Zhi along with Liu Bang’s parents were released.
The following year, Liu Bang proclaimed himself emperor and established Lü Zhi as Empress. Upon assuming the position of empress, she secretly wielded fortune and authority. She possessed a resolute, strategic, and steadfast character, but was also ruthless. She assisted Emperor Gaozu in pacifying the empire, and many of the high-ranking ministers who were executed met their fate largely due to her influence and actions. In the tenth year of Emperor Gaozu’s reign (197 BCE), Chen Xi rebelled. Liu Bang personally led troops to suppress the rebellion, while Lü Zhi remained in Chang’an. She conspired with Xiao He and had Han Xin executed on charges of collaborating with Chen Xi’s rebellion, leading to the extermination of his three clans.
When Liu Bang attacked Chen Xi and reached Handan, he summoned troops from Peng Yue. Peng Yue claimed illness and did not go, and was subsequently demoted to commoner status and exiled to Shu. Lü Zhi, believing he could not be left as a future threat, instigated others to falsely accuse Peng Yue of rebellion. As a result, he was executed, and his three clans were also exterminated.
Liu Bang considered Liu Ying too weak and intended to appoint Liu Ruyi, the son of his favored consort Consort Qi and King of Zhao, as crown prince instead. However, due to opposition from ministers and Lü Zhi’s efforts to protect Liu Ying’s position, the plan to change the crown prince failed.
After Liu Bang’s death, Liu Ying succeeded to the throne as Emperor Hui. Lü Zhi, now elevated to Empress Dowager, was free to do almost whatever she wished. From this point on, the emperor resided in Weiyang Palace, under the protection of the Northern and Southern guards, while the Empress Dowager lived in Changle Palace, under the protection of her own security forces, and Southern guard; When officials submitted memorials, everything was prepared in duplicate—one copy was submitted to the Empress Dowager, and the other to the emperor. This created a situation of ‘two sovereigns’ (两主, Liǎng zhǔ). She poisoned Liu Ruyi, the King of Zhao, cruelly murdered Consort Qi, and also persecuted other imperial princes of the Liu family. From 194 BCE onward, Emperor Hui withdrew from exercising power, and Empress Lü effectively assumed the role of regent. At this time, Lü Gengshi, the commander of the Changle Palace guards, and a man surnamed "Zuo" were the commander of the Weiyang Palace guards, and both were her allies. Emperor Hui, distressed by Lü Zhi’s actions, eventually died of illness brought on by grief.
Lü Zhi then assumed regency and moved to Weiyang Palace. a
All decrees and orders were issued by her; she was, in everything except name, the emperor. She successively enthroned the young emperors Qianshao and Houshao, and enfeoffed her nephews Lü Tai, Lü Chan, Lü Lu, and Lü Tong as kings, assigning them respectively to the kingdoms of Lu, Liang, Zhao, and Yan, and she also enfeoffed six other members of her clan as marquises; both of these actions were contrary to the "Oath of the White Horse". She sidelined veteran ministers such as Wang Ling and promoted her close associates. Then, in the later years of Empress Lü, Lü Chan and Lü Lu came to monopolize state power. Internally, they controlled both imperial armies; externally, they governed the regions of Liang and Zhao. Arrogantly, they made all major decisions themselves, settling affairs within the palace precincts. Moreover, her younger sister, Lü Xu, relied on the favor of Empress Lü to move freely in and out of the palace. Lü Xu would speak highly of her associates while slandering her opponents, exerting significant influence over judgments concerning rewards and punishments. Displaying arrogance and self-will, she demonstrated considerable power. She was appointed by her sister, Empress Lü, to the unprecedented position of Marquis of Lingguang — an honor highly unusual for a woman — and amassed great wealth. The concentration of power within the Lü clan and their despotic conduct led to the oppression of those below and the marginalization of high-ranking officials, chilling the hearts of people throughout the realm. The history of this 8-year period (188-180 BC) is considered and recognized as the reign of Empress Dowager Lü. She dominated the political scene for 15 years until her death in August 180 BC, and is often depicted as the first woman to have ruled China. 
In the eighth year of Empress Gao’s reign (August, 180 BCE), Lü Zhi died (according to one theory, she died of rabies; see the “Anecdotes – dying from dog disaster” section). Before her death, she made arrangements. First, she appointed Lü Lü, the King of Zhao, who at that time commanded the Northern Army (军北军, Jūn běi jūn), as Supreme Commander (上将军, Shàng jiàngjūn) so that he would control all military forces of the empire, both internal and external. She also ordered Lü Chan, the King of Liang, who had previously been in command of the Southern Army (居南军, Jū nán jūn), to be appointed as Chancellor (相国, xiàngguó) so that he would take control of the imperial secretariat. Empress Lü further warned them not to attend her funeral after her death, but instead to keep their forces in place and remain stationed to protect the palace and the capital, Chang’an, so that they would not be disarmed or brought under control by members of the Liu clan and ministers who opposed the Lü faction. Empress Lü died shortly thereafter. On her deathbed, she also arranged for Lü Lü’s daughter to be made empress of the young Emperor Houshao. She also issued an imperial decree (詔制, zhào zhì) that the Imperial Seal (傳國玉璽, Chuán guó yù xǐ) be handed over to the young emperor, and simultaneously appointed Shen Yiji (審食其), the Left Chancellor (左丞相, Zuǒ chéngxiàng), as Grand Tutor (太傅, Taifu), entrusting him with the responsibility of educating the emperor. However, the arrangements she made were not sufficient to prevent disaster, as the Grand Commandant Zhou Bo, Chancellor Chen Ping, and Marquis of Zhuxu Liu Zhang swiftly eliminated the Lü clan.
During the eight years of Lü Zhi’s regency, she continued the policies of rest and recuperation for the people initiated under Emperor Gaozu of Han. She encouraged agriculture, abolished harsh laws such as the extermination of three clans and the law against heretical speech, laying the foundation for the Rule of Wen and Jing. While four women are noted as having been politically active before her—Fu Hao, Yi Jiang, Lady Nanzi, and Queen Dowager Xuan—Lü was perhaps the first woman to have ruled over united China. Empress Lü restrained herself from making arrangements to have herself declared empress regnant. Her course of action was copied during the Later Han period and on the several occasions in subsequent dynasties when China was dominated by an empress dowager. But she enjoyed unquestioned power. Of course, it was never repeated until the rise of Wu Zetian, who also surpassed her.
